dhq:abstract.p: The increasing reliance on open-source datasets for training large language models has revealed a critical oversight in artificial intelligence development: the presence of historical toxicity embedded within canonical literary texts. This article examines the application of contemporary toxicity detection models to the Chanson de Roland, one of medieval French foundational literary works, exposing significant challenges in identifying hate speech, violence advocacy, and discriminatory content within historical documents. Using the multilingual Detoxify model on Joseph Bédier's modern French translation, I analyze 2,605 sentences to assess how toxicity detection models trained primarily on contemporary social media content perform when evaluating medieval literature. My findings reveal a troubling pattern: While the model successfully flags some explicit threats and insults, it systematically fails to detect the text's most problematic content, including religious misrepresentation, forced conversion narratives, and anti-Black racism. These false negatives represent a fundamental problem for AI models being trained on historical open data, as they risk perpetuating and amplifying centuries-old discriminatory frameworks while appearing objective. This research contributes to urgent debates about responsible AI development, arguing that without human-annotated ground truth datasets specifically designed for historical texts toxicity, current LLMs risk distorting historical understanding and diffusing undetected violent and racist discrimination at unprecedented scale. I advocate for interdisciplinary collaboration between computer scientists and humanities scholars to develop ethical frameworks for curating historical datasets that acknowledge their toxic content without either sanitizing history or amplifying historical harm.

div.head: 1. Introduction
div.p: The contemporary landscape of artificial intelligence development faces an emerging crisis that threatens both technological ethics and historical understanding. As companies race to build increasingly sophisticated large language models, the source material for training these systems has become a critical concern. Following high-profile controversies over copyright infringement and data provenance, several AI-development initiatives have pivoted toward using exclusively open-source, public-domain datasets (Langlais et al. 2025a; Baack et al. 2025). While this shift addresses legitimate concerns about intellectual-property rights, it has inadvertently created a new and potentially more insidious problem: the wholesale incorporation of historical toxicity into the foundational training data of next-generation AI systems.

Historical texts, by virtue of their age, overwhelmingly exist in the digital public domain. From medieval manuscripts to early twentieth-century 20th Century newspapers, from colonial administrative records to canonical literary works, these documents represent centuries of human culture, knowledge, and expression. Yet they also encode the prejudices, violence, and discriminatory ideologies of their eras. European medievalMedieval literature contains, among other things, virulent IslamophobicIslamophobia and antisemitic rhetoric and calls for assaulting and mass-murdering murdering of non-Christians. Nineteenth-century scientific texts propagate theories of biological racism. Colonial documents normalisenormalize slavery and genocide, and defend Europeana European, supremacy over other populations. These are not merely unfortunate historical artefactsartifacts to be contextualisedcontextualized by scholars; when incorporated into AI training datasets without proper curation, they become active ingredients in shaping how artificial-intelligence systems “understand” human language, culture, and values.

Large language models do not neutrally learn from training data; rather, they statistically encode and often amplify the biases, stereotypes, and discriminatory patterns present in that data. Empirical research has documented that language models trained on internet-scale corpora reproduce harmful stereotypes related to gender, race, religion, and national origin at rates comparable to or exceeding those found in the training data itself (Bolukbasi et al., 2016; Abid et al., 2021). More concerning, recent research suggests that scaling the process of scaling language models can amplify rather than mitigate these biases: as models grow increase in size and are trained on larger and more diverse datasets, they may develop more sophisticated and less easily detectable mechanisms for encoding discriminatory patterns (Bender et al. 2021; Gupta and Ranjan 2024; Ranjan, 2021, Gupta et al. 2024, Rajan et al. 2024). In particular, Abid and colleagues’' analysis of persistent anti-Muslim bias in large language models demonstrates that models trained on standard internet corpora systematically associate Islamic terms with negative sentiment and violent concepts, reproducing centuries-old Orientalist tropes and contemporary Islamophobic discourse (Abid et al., 2021). These findings raise urgent questions about what happens when historical texts, , which themselves encode medieval patterns of discrimination, racialisation,racialization and religious domination, enter , are incorporated into training data without explicit recognition of the discriminatory patterns they contain. Contemporary models will not simply “learn”"learn" medieval data as historical artefact; artifact; rather, they will learn to reproduce and naturalisenaturalize historical patterns of discrimination, making those patterns available to contemporary users and systems as normal and acceptable linguistic associations (Langlais et al., 2025b; Arnett et al., 2024).

This tension occurs within a broader awakening, over the past decade, to the role of medieval and historical content in contemporary political discourse in the last ten years. The events at Charlottesville in 2017, where white-supremacist groups openly deployed medieval symbolism and rhetoric, served as a watershed moment for medieval studies (Elliott 2018; Blake 2020). Medieval epic texts, with its explicit calls for violence against Muslims and its celebration of forced conversion and subjugationconversions and subjugations, has proven particularly attractive to contemporary movements seeking historical legitimation for their hatredhate (Van Hemelryck 2009). PremodernMedieval Critical Race Studies has emerged as a vital field addressing these concerns, with scholars such as like Geraldine Heng, Cord Whitaker, Jeffrey Jerome Cohen, John Tolan, and Sharon Kinoshita , among others, examining how race-thinking, religious othering, and discriminatory frameworks operated in premodern contexts (Cohen 2001; Kinoshita 2006; Heng 2018; Whitaker 2019; , Tolan 2023; Whitaker 2019, Whitaker et al. 2024; Whitaker 2025). Recent scholarship has also shownhighlighted how medieval literature encoded forms of discrimination beyond religious intolerance, including homophobia and gender-based violence (Wade 2025).

The intersection of these historical concerns with AI artificial intelligence development creates unprecedented challenges. When AI systems trained on medieval texts reproduce historical biases at scale, they risk perpetuating the perpetuation of medieval discriminatory frameworks through ostensibly neutral technological systems. Unlike human readers, who can contextualisecontextualize historical content, AI models trained on such material may internaliseinternalize and replicate these patterns without critical awareness.

A single example illustrates what is at stake. When Roland confronts an enemy contingent, the poem describes them as “la gent maudite, qui est plus noire que l’encre et qui n’a rien de blanc que les dents” (the cursed people, who are blacker than ink and have nothing white except their teeth). The line fuses dark skin, moral curse, and dehumanisation in a single image, immediately before a scene of killing. As the analysis below shows, the Detoxify model assigns this passage a score well below the flagging threshold. The most dangerous content in the Chanson de Roland is frequently the content that contemporary detection systems are least equipped to see.

This article addresses these concerns through a case study of one of Europe's most influential medieval texts: the Chanson de Roland, a text that celebrates violence against Muslims, advocates forced conversion, depicts mass slaughter with aesthetic pleasure, and contains explicitly racist and hateful characterizations of African and Middle Eastern peoples. When such a text enters AI training datasets without adequate toxicity flagging, what implications does this have for the systems that are built?

This article therefore addresses these concerns through a case study of one of Europe’s most influential medieval texts: investigates the application of a contemporary toxicity detection model to medieval literature, specifically examining the Chanson de Roland, a poem that celebrates violence against Muslims, advocates forced conversion, depicts mass slaughter with aesthetic pleasure, and contains explicitly racist and theologically prejudiced characterisations of Muslims, African and Middle Eastern peoples. When such a text enters AI training datasets without adequate toxicity flagging, what are the implications for the systems built upon it? I map a contemporary toxicity-detection model’ by mapping the model's performance across the model’s six toxicity sub-categories and identify both its identifying both successes and its systematic failures. I argue that these failures reveal a fundamental problem in how AI artificial intelligence systems approach historical texts: models trained on contemporary social-media data encounter historical discourse through contemporary moderation priorities, filtering out precisely those forms of structural violence that were most consequential in their medieval context. Whether artificial intelligence can ever be made fully “ethical” or “responsible” is a question I return to in the conclusion; my argument here is narrower and, I think more tractable, that responsibility in this domain is at minimum a matter of recognising, documenting, and reducing the harms that uncurated historical data introduces. To that end I advocate This raises urgent questions for responsible AI development. When historical texts encoding racialized religious domination and forced conversion are incorporated into training corpora without explicit scholarly attention to these patterns, resulting models will learn to reproduce and naturalize centuries-old forms of domination. We therefore advocate for genuine interdisciplinary collaboration in which the humanities play a central roleHumanities play central roles in data curation and AI model development.

div.head: 2. Open Data, Dirty Data?
div.p: The debate over AI training data has intensified with growing awareness of both copyright and ethical concerns. Research on LLM copyright compliance reveals that current systems often fail to respect intellectual-property boundaries, but the focus has remained primarily on protecting contemporary creators rather than examining the ethical implications of public-domain content (Tian-Zheng Wei et al. 2025; Chen et al. 2025). The Common Corpus project represents an attempt to address these concerns through careful curation, but questions remain about how effectively toxicity can be filtered from historical materials (Langlais et al. 2025b). Chafetz and colleagueset al. argue that we may be entering a “fourth wave”"fourth wave" of open data characterisedcharacterized by the challenges posed by generative AI, requiring new frameworks for understanding data ethics (Chafetz et al. 2024). This framing matters directly for the present study: the fourth wave reconceives : "Improving transparency and documentation of open data not as just a static public good but as raw material for generative AI models, which is precisely the point at which undetected historical toxicity stops being a a note in a datasheet and becomes a training-data problem with downstream consequences. As Chafetz and colleagues put it, improved transparency and documentation across the data lifecycle can help can not only foster ethical and responsible use throughout the data lifecycle, but can also help data holders and users to better evaluate the lineage, quality, and impact of what they release the output "(Chafetz et al. 2024, p. 12), but, as I argue below, transparency about provenance does nothing on its own to surface the discrimination embedded in the content12).

CurrentThese toxicity detection systems , however, are not designed for historical content. The dominant models in the field, including Perspective API, Detoxify, and various BERT-based classifiers, were trained primarily on contemporary social media data, particularly Twitter posts and online comments (Founta et al. 2018; Vidgen et al. 2021; Wulczyn et al. 2017). These datasets capture contemporary expressions of toxicity but may fail to recognize historical forms of hate speech, particularly when expressed in formal or literary language. This is why medieval poetry and philosophical treatises pose a distinctive problem for automated detection: their discriminatory content is encoded through epic lines, theological argument, and chivalric convention rather than through the direct, informal slurs on which the models were trained, a point developed in Section 3 and demonstrated empirically in Section 5. Research on large webtextweb text corpora like C4 (Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus) has revealed significant toxicity in contemporary internet data and LLMs, but less attention has been paid to historical materials (Gehman et al. 2020, Dodge et al. 2021). Recent work on global hate speech datasets demonstrates the challenge of identifying toxicity across cultural and linguistic contexts, but temporal variation remains underexplored (Tonneau et al. 2025).

The contemporary emphasis on "ethical AI" through open data initiatives rests on a fundamental but unexamined assumption: that transparency and accessibility of data sources constitute responsible practice. Yet as historian Jo Guldi argues, data, and particularly historical data is inherently "dirty": it carries within it the embedded biases, power, inconsistencies, erasure and ideological commitments of those who created, collected, and preserved it (Guldi, 2023). "Openness" about data sources does not clean this dirtiness; rather, it risks amplifying it. Guldi's concept of dirty data thus reframes a crucial question: the problem is not whether historical data is hidden or transparent, but rather whether we engage with it with full recognition of what Guldi identifies as the "danger" of data mining: the risk that we will treat computational analysis as neutral extraction of truth from historical materials, failing to recognize that the materials themselves encode centuries of domination, that our analytical methods carry their own ideological commitments, and that the act of training AI systems on "open" historical data may accomplish a particular form of epistemic violence: the naturalization of historical oppression through computational legitimacy (Guldi, 2023, pp.37-43).

The Pleias team's own research acknowledges the toxicity problem in open-source pretraining data, particularly in nineteenth-century American newspaper collections (Arnett et al. 2024). Their analysis of these historical materials revealed patterns of racism, xenophobia, and other forms of discrimination that contemporary toxicity filters often failed to detect. This finding is particularly concerning given that newspapers represent relatively straightforward prose compared to complex literary works. If toxicity detection fails for modern journalistic content, how much more severely will it fail for allegorical poetry, epic verse, or philosophical treatises from medieval or pre-modern texts?

This research argues for an urgent shift in how we approach historical data in AI development. We cannot simply apply contemporary toxicity filters to medieval texts and assume the problem is solved. Nor can we sanitisze historical datasets by removing all problematic content, as this would constitute a different form of historical distortion. Instead, we need human-annotated ground truth datasets specifically designed for pre-modernhistorical texts, developed through collaboration between computer scientists and humanities scholars. We also need more sophisticated AI models capable of recognizing that discrimination takes different forms across time and culture. Most fundamentally, we need tomust acknowledge that transparency about training data is necessary but insufficient; it must be acompagnied by we must also ensure that transparency includes clear reflexion documentation onf historical toxicity and its potential impacts to our present and future.

div.head: The stakes could not be higher. As AI systems become increasingly integrated into education, information retrieval, content creation, and decision-making processes, the historical biases they encode will shape how future generations understand the past and conceptualize human diversity. We face a choice: develop responsible frameworks for handling historical toxicity in AI training data now, or risk building systems that amplify centuries-old discrimination at a scale and speed unprecedented in human history. This article contributes to that urgent project by demonstrating both the limitations of current approaches and the path toward more responsible alternatives.
3. Toxicity Detection Models and Their Limitations for Historical Content
div.p: The contemporary landscape of toxicity detection in natural-language processing represents a remarkable technical achievement, but one built on foundations that may be fundamentally unsuited tofor historical text analysis. Understanding the architecture, training data, and intended applications of current toxicity detection systems is essential for evaluating their performance on medieval materials and recognisingrecognizing where they systematically fail.

Because this article moves between computational and literary analysis, a few terms used throughout deserve plain definitions at the outset for readers who are not specialists in machine learning. A toxicity score is a number between 0 and 1 that an automated model assigns to a passage, expressing its estimated probability that the passage contains a given kind of harmful content. A threshold is the cut-off above which a passage is treated as flagged; 0.5 is a common choice in content-moderation systems. A false positive is benign content the model wrongly flags as toxic, and a false negative (the central concern of this article) is genuinely toxic content the model fails to flag. By human-annotated ground-truth datasets I mean datasets in which domain experts have manually labelled passages as toxic or not according to explicit, historically informed criteria, providing a reference standard against which automated detection can be measured and trained.

Modern toxicity detection emerged primarily in response to online harassment, hate speech, and abusive behaviour behavior proliferated in digital spaces, asand companies and researchers sought automated methods to identify and filter harmful content at scale. The technical approaches have evolved from simple keyword filtering to sophisticated machine-learning models, but the core assumption has remained constant: toxicity is defined primarily through contemporary social norms as expressed in online interactions. The foundational datasets for toxicity detection reflect this origin. The Twitter Abusive BehaviourBehavior dataset compiled by Founta and colleagues represents one of the earliest large-scale efforts, using crowdsourcing to label tweets across categories of abuse (Founta et al. 2018). The Contextual Abuse Dataset extended (CAD) expanded this work by incorporating more nuanced contextual information about when and why language might be considered abusive (Vidgen et al. 2021). Google’'s Perspective API, one of the most widely used toxicity detection systems, was trained on comment threads from platforms such as like Wikipedia and The New York Times, focusing on personal attacks and aggressive language (Wulczyn et al. 2017). The Common Crawl corpus, used extensively in language model training, has been analysed for toxicity, revealing significant prevalence of problematic content in contemporary web data (Dodge et al. 2021).

These datasets share several characteristics that make them poorly suited for historical analysis. First, they capture language as it appears in informal, often confrontational online contexts. Social media discourse operates under different linguistic conventions than formal literature, with directness, brevity, and emotional intensity valued over the rhetorical literary elaboration common in medieval texts. Second, the datasets reflect contemporary cultural frameworks for understanding identity, discrimination, and harm. Categories like identity attack are defined through current awareness of racism, sexism, homophobia, and other forms of bigotry, but these frameworks do not map cleanly onto pre-modern forms of discrimination. Third, the temporal scope is extremely narrow, typically covering only the past decade or two of online discourse. This makes the models highly attuned to recent slurs, contemporary political conflicts, and current manifestations of hate speech, but almost definitely blind to historical expressions of similar sentiments.

Recent efforts to broaden coverage expand toxicity detection to more diverse contexts have begun to acknowledge some of these limitations. The HateDay dataset offers insights intoprovides insights from global hate speech on Twitter, showingdemonstrating how toxicity varies across linguistic and cultural contexts (Tonneau et al. 2025), and multilingual detoxification projects have expanded coverage across languages (Dementieva et al. 2025). Yet this work still draws on contemporary sources and does not address temporal variation or historical content. Multilingual toxicity detection projects have expanded coverage across languages, but again with datasets drawn from contemporary sources (Dementieva et al. 2025).

This limitation also connects to broader debates about bias and fairness in AI development. Research on algorithmic bias has demonstrated that discrimination often operates not through overtly prejudiced rules but through the reproduction of patterns present in training data (Noble 2018; Benjamin 2019; Buolamwini 2024). Safiya Noble’s analysis of search engines demonstrates how ostensibly neutral ranking systems encode and amplify racism through the data and the design choices behind them, so that the bias appears as a property of the algorithm rather than of the society and archives it learns from (Noble 2018). Ruha Benjamin’s account of the “New Jim Code” extends the point: discriminatory outcomes are routinely reproduced by technologies marketed as objective, efficient, and even progressive, precisely because their neutrality is assumed rather than examined (Benjamin 2019). Joy Buolamwini’s work on facial-analysis systems similarly shows how unrepresentative data produces systems that fail unevenly across populations (Buolamwini 2024). However, these approaches face significant challenges when applied to historical content. 43. The Chanson de Roland: A Case Study in Medieval Toxicity
div.p: The Chanson de Roland occupies a unique and troubling position in European cultural history. Celebrated as one of the first major texts composed in French rather than Latin, the poem has been central to French national identity since its nineteenth-century rediscovery rediscovery in the nineteenth century (Van Hemelryck 2009; MosserMoser 2015). It has been translated into dozens of languages, taught in schools across Europe and beyond, and analysedanalyzed in countless scholarly works. The Oxford manuscript, version, dating from the beginning first half of the twelfth century, is12th C., represents the oldest surviving version of a narrative that evidently circulated in multiple forms throughout medieval Europe. For students of medieval literature, it , the Chanson de Rolandis essential reading:, a foundational text for understanding the development of vernacular European literature, epic poetry conventions, and medieval narrative structures.

Yet, the poem is also, in Jean-Charles Payen’'s provocative formulation, a “"poétique du génocide joyeux” — " – a poetics of joyful genocide (Payen 1979). It The text celebrates religious violence with aesthetic pleasure, depicts mass slaughter in elaborate detail, advocates the forced conversion or extermination of wholedifferent populations, and characterisescharacterizes non-Christians through explicitly racist and theologically prejudiced frameworks. The Christian Frankish characters are consistently portrayed as righteous, brave, and favouredfavored by God, while their MuslimMuslims opponents are depicted as treacherous, cowardly, and spiritually damned. Violence against Muslims is not merely justified but and glorified; conversion or death are presented as the only acceptable outcomes of Christian–Muslim confrontations.

Understanding the Chanson de Roland's toxicity requires situating the text within its historical context. The poemIt was likely composed in the late eleventh or early twelfth century, shortly after the First Crusade (1095-1099). Although it purports to recount events from Charlemagne’s reign, specifically his Spanish campaigns and the supposed ambush of his rearguard at Roncevaux in 778, its composition in the Crusade era fundamentally shaped its ideological framework. While the narrative purports to recount events from the reign of Charlemagne in the late eighth century and specifically Charlemagne's campaigns in Spain and the Battle of Roncevaux Pass in 778 where Charlemagne's rearguard was supposedly ambushed and destroyed, the poem's composition in the Crusade era fundamentally shaped its ideological framework. Written roughly three centuries after the events it depicts, the Chanson de Roland is less a chronicle than a complete ideological rewriting of eighth-century military history through the lens of twelfth-century crusading geopolitics and Reconquista ideology. By the time of its likely composition, Christian kingdoms in Iberia were actively at war against the Muslim kingdom of al-Andalus, a process that would shape Christian self-understanding across Western Europe (García-Guijarro Ramos 2016).

div.head: 54.1 Applying Contemporary Toxicity Detection to Historical Text
div.p: My methodological approach to analyzing the Chanson de Roland emerged from the need to test rigorously test how contemporary AI-based toxicity detection systems performs on historical medieval literary content. While previous research has examined toxicity in historical newspaper corpora (Arnett et al. 2024), no systematic analysis has evaluated these systems' performance on medieval epic poetry. OurThis study fills theis gap through computational analysis of Joseph Bédier's widely circulated modern French translation of the Chanson de Roland (Bedier 1922), using employing the Detoxify model to assess its 2,605 sentences across seven toxicity categories.

The choice of text version represented a crucial initial decision. The Chanson de Roland exists in multiple manuscript versions with textual variations, and numerous translations into modern languages have been produced since the nineteenth century. IWe selected Bédier's translation for several compelling reasons (Bedier 1922). First, it has achieved canonical status in French literary culture and remains one of the most widely taught and read versions of the text and was one of the first prose translations of the text in prose (Lucken 2018). Second, it is clearly in the public domain and widely available as open data on internet platforms such as Wikisource, making it precisely the kind of historical text that might be incorporated into AI training datasets without careful curation. Third, by analyszing a modern French translation in prose rather than the original versed Old French originaltext, Iwe eliminate the confounding variable variations of medieval language forms, allowing us to focus on how toxicity detection performs on accessible, readable French rather than archaic medieval linguistic structures that might independently affect model performance.

The decision to analyze a translation rather than the original text deserves further elaboration, as it has both advantages and limitations for our research questions. Analyzing the Old French original would provide insights into how toxicity detection performs on genuinely historical language with ancient vocabulary, grammatical structures, and semantic frameworks. However, such analysis would make it impossible to disentangle failures due to medieval linguistic features from failures due to conceptual or ideological differences. If the Detoxify model failed to flag problematic content in Old French, we could not determine whether this reflected the model's inability to process medieval language or its inability to recognize medieval forms of discrimination. By analyzing Bédier's modern French translation, we ensure that language is comprehensible to contemporary French speakers and that any failures to detect toxicity reflect conceptual rather than purely linguistic limitations.Additionally, from the perspective of AI training data, translations like Bédier's represent the most likely form in which medieval texts would enter training corpora. While some AI systems might be trained on Old French texts for specialized applications, the vast majority of users and training datasets would encounter medieval literature through translations into modern languages. Thus, understanding how toxicity detection performs on widely-circulated translations has direct relevance for evaluating the risks of including such materials in training datasets.

IWe obtained the Bédier translation as plain text from its Wikisource edition (https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/La_Chanson_de_Roland/Joseph_B%C3%A9dier/La_Chanson_de_Roland/Traduction, last consulted 9 December 2025 ). The text wasand preprocessed it to remove editorial apparatus such as stanza markers. IWe segmented the text into sentences using SpaCy Sentencizer, resulting in 2,605 sentences for analysis. Each sentence was assigned a unique identifier corresponding to its position in the text (sentence ID), allowing to track specific passages through the analysis and return to them in their narrative context. SThis sentence-level granularity was chosen to preserve meaningful context while allowing detailed examination of specific passages. Analyzing at the: word or phrase level analysis would have stripped away too much context, while analyzing entire sections or chapters level analysis would have averaged out variation and made it impossible to identify specific toxic passages. Each sentence was assigned a unique identifier corresponding to its position in the text, allowing us to track specific passages through the analysis and return to them in their narrative context. This identification system proved crucial for the detailed error analysis presented in the results section, where we examine particular sentences that represent successful detection, false positives, or false negatives.

For the toxicity detection analysisitself, Iwe employed used the multilingual Detoxify model, specifically the multilingual version capable of processing French text (Hanu 2020) which output. These scores range from 0 to 1, with higher scores indicating greater probability that the text contains the specified type of toxicity. The model outputs raw probability scores rather than binary classifications, allowing for nuanced analysis of borderline cases and threshold-dependent interpretation.Following common practice, We I treated 0.5 as the flagging identified sentences exceeding threshold values of 0.5, common cutoff used in content moderation applications.

Identifying false negatives (toxic passages the model fails to flag) required an explicit, historically informed ground-truth procedure, since the whole argument turns on the gap between expert and model judgement. I first read the full Bédier's translation as a domain specialist in medieval French literature and flagged every passage meeting one or more predefined criteria for historical toxicity: (i) theological misrepresentation of a religious group (for example, attributing polytheism to Muslims); (ii) advocacy, celebration, or matter-of-fact narration of religiously or ethnically targeted violence; (iii) racialised physical description linking bodily features to moral or spiritual status; and (iv) the representation of forced conversion as legitimate or salvific. I then compared this expert annotation against the Detoxify scores for the same sentences. A false negative was recorded where a passage met at least one criterion yet scored below the 0.5 threshold in every category. Because the judgements of a single annotator necessarily involve interpretation, borderline cases were treated conservatively (counted as toxic only where the criteria were clearly met) and the qualitative discussion below quotes each passage in full so that readers can assess the classification for themselves. The criteria are derived from, and consistent with, the scholarship on medieval Islamophobia and premodern race-thinking discussed in the sections above.

This independent sentence-level analysis has both strengths and limitations. The strength is that Iit allows precise identification of which specific passages trigger toxicity detection and facilitates comparison across categories and severity levels. The limitation is thatBut it also removes broader narrative context that might affect human judgment about whether content is problematic. A sentence describing violence in isolation might be judged differently than the same sentence understood as part of a broader pattern of celebrated violence against a specific religious or ethnic group. However, because AI training data is typically processed in chunks rather than whole books, sentence-level analysis is a reasonable proxy for the sub-document units in which models encounter texts (Ding 2024).However, since AI training data is typically processed in relatively small chunks (sentences, paragraphs, or short passages) rather than entire books, our sentence-level analysis reflects how AI systems would actually encounter this content in practice.

The interpretive framework for our results acknowledges several limitations inherent in this approachOther limitations should be acknowledged. On one hand, ourThe analysis relies on a single toxicity detection model -, though Detoxify is a sophisticated, widely-used, multilingual approach to toxicity detection - and different models might perform differently. However, Detoxify represents a sophisticated, widely-used, multilingual approach to toxicity detection and thus offers a reasonable proxy for current state-of-the-art capabilities. On the other hand , our My ground truth judgments about which sentences are actually toxictoxic reflect scholarly expertise but nonetheless involve interpretive judgment. Different readers might disagree about borderline cases or about how to weigh different forms of toxicity. Lastly, the our sentence-level analysis necessarily loses some narrative context that affects human understanding of the text. These limitations notwithstanding, our this methodology still provides rigorous empirical evidence about how contemporary machine learning systems handle medieval toxic content.

div.head: 54.4 False Positives: When the Model Misfires

div.p: False positives, non-toxic content wrongly flagged, , where the model incorrectly flags non-toxic content, reveal systematic problems with applying contemporary toxicity detection to medievalancient texts. They fall into three typesOur analysis identified three primary categories of false positives: archaic or ambiguous vocabulary read through misinterpreted based on modern meanings, subjunctive or conditional verbs verb forms misread as direct threats, and accumulations of geographic or ethnic terms triggering identity-attack detection despite benign usage in context.

The most striking false positive case involves the obscenity category's second-highest score (0.5368) for the sentence "Tant de hampes se brisent, tant d'épieux fourbis!" (So many shafts break, so many polished spears!). The model flags this as obscene, apparently interpreting "fourbis" based on modern French usage where "fourbi" can be vulgar slang for "stuff" or have sexual connotations in certain contexts (see Fourbir in the Wikitonary https://fr.wiktionary.org/wiki/fourbir, consulted on 5 December 2025). However, in this sentence, "fourbi" functions as a past participle of "fourbir" (to polish/burnish), describing polished or well-maintained spears. This represents semantic drift,: a word that had historical neutral or positive meaning in the historical text has acquired vulgar associations in contemporary usage, causesing the model to misinterpret the historical usage. This error type is particularly problematic because it would lead AI systems to flag or filter content that is genuinely innocuous in its historical context.

Another A second significant false positive involves subjunctive mood misinterpretation.. The sentence "Lle roi Marsile eût été tué ou pris" (King Marsile would have been killed or captured) scores 0.7073 for threat. This sentence employs the past subjunctive ("eût été") to describe a hypothetical alternative history: what would have happened if events had unfolded differently and. It does not advocate killing or capturing Marsile; it speculates about an alternative outcome. However, the model's pattern matching identifies keywords like "tué" (killed) in near a proper proximity to a person's name and interprets this as threatening regardless of grammatical mood or conditional context. This reveals a fundamental limitation: the model was trained on social media data where conditional statements are often used to express genuine threats ("if X happens, I'll kill them"), but it cannot distinguish such genuine threats from literary use of subjunctive mood to explore hypothetical scenarios.

This sentence enumerates geographic and ethnic groups that might rebel against Charlemagne. While it includes the problematic term "maudits" (cursed) as a clear identity attack, there is no clear explanation about why the high obscenity score appears to be triggered primarily by the accumulation of ethnic and geographic terms.

Collectively, tThese false positives collectively demonstrate that current toxicity detection models are optimized for contemporary contexts and perform poorly on medieval texts,. The models misinterpreting archaic ancient language, cannot handle complex grammatical moods, and overgeneraliszinge from contemporary hate speech patterns, and fail to distinguish narrative description from direct advocacy. Each false positive represents a case where an AI system would incorrectly filter or flag historical content, potentially distorting users' access to these materials. However, as troubling as false positives are, the false negatives, genuinely toxic content that the model completely misses, represent an even more serious problem.

The passage explicitly links skin color ("noir que poix fondue") to moral depravity ("vices," "crimes"), theological error ("il ne croit pas en Dieu"), and criminal inclination ("il aime le meurtre et la traîtrise"). It then concludes by explaining that Archbishop Turpin desires to kill him ("Le mieux, de beaucoup, est que j'aille l'occire"), presenting this racist characterization as justification for violence by one of the highest members of the Church.

This represents precisely the kind of content that should trigger maximum toxicity detection: explicit racism linking Black people to evil, presented as justification for killing. Yet the model largely fails to detect it. Why? Because racism is expressed through formal, literary language employing similes and theological frameworks rather than contemporary racial slurs. The passage does not use modern racist terms but instead employs medieval Christian vocabulary of vice and virtue, historical color metaphors, and literary description. Current AI systems trained primarily on contemporary social media cannot recognize this as racism because they have not been taught that historical forms of racial discrimination look different from contemporary expressions.

The systematic use of Sarrasin (Saracen) throughout the text presents another layer of erasure. Medieval usage of "Sarrasin" to describe Muslims represents a deliberate choice that others and depoliticizes Islamic peoples, reducing diverse Muslim societies to a single homogenic category defined from a Christian European perspective. Modern scholarship on medieval Islamophobia has documented how terminology like "Sarrasin" functioned to erase Muslim political, cultural, and religious complexity and agency while facilitating violence through categorical othering (Rajabzadeh 2019). Yet not a single instance of "Sarrasin" in the text triggers toxicity detection because the term appears neutral to contemporary AI systems unaware of its historical function.

The most harmful historical content often appears in the most formally legitimate language of its period. The implications extend well beyond one poem: if a heavily beyond the Chanson de Roland to all historical texts entering AI training datasets. As these materials enter AI training datasets at scale, the accumulated undetected historical toxicity may fundamentally shape how AI systems understand otherness, religious diversity, race, and the legitimacy of violence.

div.head: 6. Conclusion: Toward Responsible Historical Data Curation?
div.p: These findings call The findings presented in this article ask for immediate attention from the AI-artificial intelligence research community, humanists, digital humanists, and policymakers concerned with AI ethics. Current Our analysis demonstrates that current toxicity detection systems, sophisticated as they are while sophisticated for contemporary social media content, are fundamentally inadequate for identifying harmful content in historical texts. The Chanson de Roland case study reveals systematic blind spots where medieval religious fanaticism, forced-conversion advocacy, and racist characterisationcharacterization pass undetected through standard AI filtering systems. As AI development accelerates toward training ever-larger models trained on public-language models on increasingly comprehensive datasets drawn from public domain historical materials, this iswe face an urgent problem forcrisis that threatens both technological ethics and historical understanding.

The scale of the problem cannot be overstated. Millions of historical documents are being digitiseddigitized and released as open data, celebrated for widening access to making cultural heritage accessible but rarely accompanied by adequate annotation of their embedded discrimination. Initiatives such as the Pleias project arecontextual annotation and curation about embedded discriminatory content. The Pleias project, Common Corpus initiative, and similar efforts represent laudable attempts to create transparent, ethically sourced training data AI training data, but our research demonstrates that transparency alone is insufficient (Langlais et al. 2025a; Langlais et al. 2025b), but this research demonstrates that transparency alone is insufficient: without detection . Without sophisticated toxicity detection specifically designed for historical content, or extensive without extensive human annotation by scholars trained to recognise historical recognize historical forms of discrimination, these open datasets risk becoming vehicles for amplifying centuries-old bigotry at unprecedented scale.

The danger is not hypothetical but immediateconcrete. Language mModels trained on historical texts without adequate curation internalize patterns of religious othering, racial categorization, gender hierarchy, and violence justification present in source materials. These patterns may not appearsurface not as overt hate speech in model outputs but rather as subtle biases in how the model represents different religious traditions, how it associates physical characteristics with moral qualities, how it frames historical conflicts, and what forms of violence it treats as legitimate or comprehensible. An AI system trained on unfiltered medieval literature might not reproduce medieval insults verbatim but could learn that religious difference justifies mass killing, that forced conversion is defensible, or that Medieval European Christian perspectives constitute neutral historical viewpoints. The false-positive problem compounds this: systems that wrongly flag benign historical content may restrict access to materials and distort users’ sense of the past, producing a double distortion in which genuinely toxic content circulates while benign historical language is filtered.The Muslim erasure we have documented in the toxicity model represents a particularly concerning pattern because it operates through terminology and theological frameworks that appear neutral to contemporary readers unfamiliar with medieval religious debates. When AI systems encounter repeated references to Muslims as "pagans" worshipping false gods, when they process narratives celebrating forced conversion, when they learn from texts that systematically misrepresent Islamic belief, they risk internalizing these frameworks as factual historical description rather than recognizing them as ideologically motivated distortion. The downstream effects could include AI systems that confidently misrepresent Islamic history and theology, that frame Christian-Muslim relations through Crusading narratives, or that reproduce medieval anti-Muslim tropes while appearing to offer objective information.

Current debates about AI training data have focused primarilycentre on copyright concerns, privacy violations, and protection rights of contemporary creators' rights (Tian-Zheng Wei et al. 2025; Chen et al. 2025). These are important issuesmatter, but our this research reveals that ethical curation of historical public domain data may be equally crucial for preventing AI harms. The fourth wave of open data characterized by generative AI requires frameworks that address not only intellectual property but also the embedded discrimination in historical materials (Chafetz et al. 2024, Arnett et al. 2024). Without such frameworks, the drive toward exclusively open-source training data may inadvertently create AI systems more biased and harmful than those trained on contemporary copyrighted content.

The urgency of these interventions cannot be overstated. We are currently in a critical window where decisions about AI training data curation will shape technological systems for decades to come.Largeanguage models being developed now, trained on historical data without adequate toxicity detection and contextual annotation, will influence countless downstream applications in education, information retrieval, content generation, and decision support. The biases they encode will be difficult to remediate once embedded in foundational models. We must act now to ensure that the historical discrimination we document does not become amplified at scale through AI systems that appear objective and authoritative while reproducing centuries-old prejudices.

Addressing these problems requires more than a call for more human oversight; it requires a shared methodological agenda, and one whose relevance extends well beyond digital humanities. Any computational project that treats historical materials as data, not only literary and documentary texts but also digitised images such as manuscripts and their illuminations, prints and photographs, maps, ethnographic and colonial imagery, caricature, and propaganda, confronts the same structural problem this article has documented in miniature. Contemporary detection systems, whether tuned to text or to images, encode present-day norms and present-day vocabularies of harm, and are therefore least able to recognise discrimination expressed in the formal conventions of another period. A racial caricature rendered in the visual grammar of nineteenth-century lithography, like the theological erasure encoded in the formal verse of the Chanson de Roland, will pass unflagged through a classifier trained on contemporary social media or modern representations. What follows is therefore proposed not as a remedy for one poem, nor for one discipline, but as a framework for the responsible use of historical text and image as training data across computational research.

I argue that the first and most important commitment is to place domain expertise at the centre of data curation and annotations rather than at its margins. Historically informed annotations produced by scholars who can read a source in its period context and who work from explicit, documented criteria of the kind set out above, rather than from contemporary moderation, should be built into curation pipelines as a matter of course; for visual materials this means involving art historians and historians of visual culture alongside textual scholars. Such annotation is most valuable when it is consolidated into period and tradition specific ground-truth corpora: human-annotated gold standards defined for clearly bounded historical, linguistic, and cultural contexts, rather than a single contemporary model presumed to fit all periods, media, and traditions at once. The workflow demonstrated here, from expert ground-truth annotation to computational scoring and error analysis, is intended precisely as a reusable template for building such corpora, and it generalises directly from text to image.

These human foundations must be matched by infrastructure and by technical research. At the level of infrastructure, the open repositories and digital archives that increasingly supply training data should adopt toxicity metadata standards that document not only a source’s lineage but the toxicity quantity it encodes and the historical circumstances of that discrimination. This operationalises the principle argued throughout this article: that transparency must extend from provenance to content, since knowing where a dataset came from is necessary but insufficient if nothing records what it contains. At the level of method, the field needs detection that is context-aware and, increasingly, multimodal and multilingual, and models able to draw on historical metadata such as date, genre, medium, and cultural setting, to recognise period-specific forms of discrimination, and to move beyond fixed contemporary lexicons and off-the-shelf image classifiers toward the multi-tiered tagging described, in which historical content is neither silently ingested nor deleted but layered with the context required to handle it responsibly.

None of this will happen at scale through goodwill alone. Funding agencies and research institutions are therefore the final, and perhaps the decisive, element: by requiring demonstrable humanities and domain expertise in any computational project that curates historical text or image data, they can ensure that such expertise is designed into projects from the outset rather than added, if at all, once the data has already been ingested. Taken together, these commitments describe a durable, cross-disciplinary practice for the years ahead. They are how the vast and growing archive of digitised human history and knowledge might become training data without laundering historical harm into systems that would otherwise reproduce it as neutral fact.

The danger is not hypothetical but immediate. Language models trained on historical texts without adequate curation internalize patterns of religious othering, racial categorization, gender hierarchy, and violence justification present in source materials. These patterns may not appear as overt hate speech in model outputs but rather as subtle biases in how the model represents different religious traditions, how it associates physical characteristics with moral qualities, how it frames historical conflicts, and what forms of violence it treats as legitimate or comprehensible. An AI system trained on unfiltered medieval literature might not reproduce medieval insults verbatim but could learn that religious difference justifies mass killing, that forced conversion is defensible, or that Medieval European Christian perspectives constitute neutral historical viewpoints.

The Muslim erasure we have documented in the toxicity model represents a particularly concerning pattern because it operates through terminology and theological frameworks that appear neutral to contemporary readers unfamiliar with medieval religious debates. When AI systems encounter repeated references to Muslims as "pagans" worshipping false gods, when they process narratives celebrating forced conversion, when they learn from texts that systematically misrepresent Islamic belief, they risk internalizing these frameworks as factual historical description rather than recognizing them as ideologically motivated distortion. The downstream effects could include AI systems that confidently misrepresent Islamic history and theology, that frame Christian-Muslim relations through Crusading narratives, or that reproduce medieval anti-Muslim tropes while appearing to offer objective information.

The racism documented in our analysis presents similar dangers. The Chanson de Roland's explicit linking of Black people to moral depravity, its stereotypical descriptions of African and Black characters, and its use of racist characterization to justify violence represent exactly the kind of historical content that has fueled scientific racism, colonial violence, and contemporary racial prejudice. When such content enters AI training datasets undetected and uncontextualized, language models may learn associations between race and moral qualities, may reproduce stereotypes about African and Black peoples, or may treat historical European perspectives on race as neutral description. Historical data offers no exception; indeed, historical texts may encode biases more insidiously because they come wrapped in cultural authority and literary prestige.

The false positive problem, while less ethically urgent than false negatives, also has serious implications. AI systems that incorrectly flag neutral historical content as toxic may restrict access to historical materials, create distorted impressions about what historical texts contain, or lead to unnecessary censorship of educational content. Students and researchers using AI tools to search historical archives might find results filtered based on inaccurate toxicity detection, missing important materials while being presented with distorted views of historical language and culture. The combination of false positives and false negatives could create a double distortion where genuinely toxic content circulates freely while benign historical language gets filtered or flagged.

Current debates about AI training data have focused primarily on copyright concerns, privacy violations, and protection of contemporary creators' rights (Tian-Zheng Wei et al. 2025; Chen et al. 2025). These are important issues, but our research reveals that ethical curation of historical public domain data may be equally crucial for preventing AI harms. The fourth wave of open data characterized by generative AI requires frameworks that address not only intellectual property but also the embedded discrimination in historical materials (Chafetz et al. 2024, Arnett et al. 2024). Without such frameworks, the drive toward exclusively open-source training data may inadvertently create AI systems more biased and harmful than those trained on contemporary copyrighted content.

Addressing these problems requires interdisciplinary collaboration and methodological innovation. We propose several urgent interventions that AI developers, digital humanists, funding agencies, and research institutions should implement immediately. These proposals operate at different scales and timelines, from immediate practical steps to longer-term research investments, but all are necessary components of responsible historical data curation.

It is worth asking directly, regarding the results of this study, whether AI can ever be ethical or responsible at all, a question the title of this section deliberately leaves open. I do not claim that it can be made fully so, and the evidence here counsel humility: a system can be transparent, open-source, and well-intentioned while still diffusing historical discrimination it cannot perceive. My argument is therefore deliberately modest. Responsibility in this domain is best understood not as a state to be achieved but as an ongoing practice of harm reduction: recognising the toxicity in our archives, documenting it, and building the human and technical infrastructure to keep it from being silently reproduced. On that understanding, the interventions above are necessary but not sufficient conditions for responsibility: a floor, not a ceiling.

Finally, a word on scope and on the limits of any single scholar’s expertise. This study has examined one text from the medieval French and Western Christian tradition, and its specific conclusions should not be over-generalised. Racism and discriminatory discourse are profoundly context-dependent: the forms they take in a crusading epic are not those they take in other linguistic, religious, and literary traditions, and no individual can be a specialist in all of them. What this article offers beyond its case study is a transferable workflow, expert ground-truth annotation paired with computational scoring and error analysis, that I hope colleagues working on other domains will take up, test, refine and criticise. The detection failures documented here are likely to recur elsewhere, but their precise shape can only be established by domain experts.

The urgency of these interventions cannot be overstated. We are currently in a critical window where decisions about AI training data curation will shape technological systems for decades to come.Largeanguage models being developed now, trained on historical data without adequate toxicity detection and contextual annotation, will influence countless downstream applications in education, information retrieval, content generation, and decision support. The biases they encode will be difficult to remediate once embedded in foundational models. We must act now to ensure that the historical discrimination we document does not become amplified at scale through AI systems that appear objective and authoritative while reproducing centuries-old prejudices.

The Chanson de Roland offers a clear warning. One of the most iconic, studied, and translatedtranslated, and analyzed medieval texts, available in carefully edited modern translationtranslations, contains systematic religious fanaticism, explicit racism, and the celebration of violence that current detection AI toxicity detection systems cannot reliably identify. If we cannot adequately handle this well-studied text, how will we handle the farvastly larger corpus of less-examined materials now entering historical materials being incorporated into AI training datasets? The answer lies in the must be through the kind of interdisciplinary collaboration, methodological innovation, and ethical commitment this article advocates. The alternative is AI systems that confidently reproduce historical patterns of discrimination while claiming neutrality, , shaping future understanding of human diversity through the unexamined prejudices of the past. We are in a narrow and consequential window: the curation decisions made now will shape foundational models, and the biases they encode for decades, and they are far harder to remediate once embedded. The case for acting now is, I think, difficult to overstate.

This research contributes to urgent debates about responsible AI development by demonstrating both the scope of the problem and the inadequacy of current solutions. We have shown that contemporary toxicity detection fails systematically when applied to historical content, that these failures produce serious ethical implications, and that new approaches are required. The path forward demands collaboration between computer scientists who understand AI systems and humanists who understand historical discrimination. It requires substantial investment in new datasets, detection methods, and annotation practices. It demands ethical frameworks that neither amplify nor erase historical toxicity but instead contextualize and curate it appropriately. Most fundamentally, it requires acknowledging that technological innovation without historical understanding risks recreating the discriminations of the past at unprecedented scale. We face a choice: develop responsible approaches to historical data now, or build AI systems that amplify centuries of violent and fanatic religious narratives while claiming objectivity. The stakes could not be higher, and the time for action is now.
